speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have had discussions with my opposite numbers in the other parties and it appears quite necessary, not only because of those discussions but because of the changed circumstances, to alter this motion. I would propose to move an amendment to the Prime Minister's motion. Without going into all the phraseology, the amended motion would make certain that the House would adjourn on Friday, July 7, tomorrow, at the regular adjournment time, but with a condition. The purpose of the condition is so that hon. members will understand that if at that moment the bill we are presently considering, Bill C-230, having to do with the resumption of operation of certain Quebec ports, has not been given Royal Assent, then the House would not adjourn. I think we all understand that if things go along normally that bill will probably be cleared, but in order to make it absolutely certain and to indicate to the country that we will not adjourn unless that matter has been attended to it seems to me a provision to that effect ought to be included in the motion. If I may, I would move the following amendment:
That the motion be amended by deleting all the words preceding the phrase "it shall stand adjourned" and substituting therefor the following words:
"That when the House adjourns at the ordinary time of daily adjournment on Friday, July 7, 1972, provided that Royal Assent has been given to Bill C-230,"
The amended paragraph would then read:
That when the House adjourns at the ordinary time of daily adjournment on Friday, July 7, 1972, provided that Royal Assent has been given to Bill C-230, it shall stand adjourned until a time to be fixed by Mr. Speaker-
And so on.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, clause 2 is the general clause. This is a piece of emergency legislation. As the minister pointed out yesterday this is the type of legislation the federal Parliament has reluctantly passed on a very limited number of occasions in the past. Hopefully, with the
St. Lawrence Ports Operations Bill
coming into effect of the Canada labour bill we recently passed there will be less and less need for this type of legislation.
Members of Parliament are handicapped in discussing this type of emergency for two major reasons. First, most of us are not familiar with either organization which is involved, whether it be the maritime shipping agencies, their component parts, or the union involved or other unions which may be indirectly involved. Yesterday the minister mentioned that a great deal of national difficulty has been created because of the closing of one of Canada's major ports. I think that is an exaggeration in an extreme sense. I am quite sure the port of Montreal is not closed. I am unfamiliar with the operation of the port authority in Montreal and, therefore, I am not too sure what authority the port council may have. I rather imagine, however, if we were really familiar with the facts rather than with what the media have reported in this particular strike, we might be less concerned than we appear to be. It is always easy to build up the argument that so many people are on strike, that the strike has continued for a certain length of time and therefore the public in some way must be affected either directly or indirectly.
It usually is a fact that the public is directly or indirectly affected. However, I imagine in this particular case the public is affected very little, and probably there have been no shipments of grain either stopped or delayed because of the strike. Some container or merchandising freight probably has suffered considerable dislocation, but this dislocation probably is to the advantage of Halifax, Saint John and other Maritime ports, including I am sure, some of the ports on the St. Lawrence Seaway which are available to ocean-going ships. Probably the ports of Hamilton and Toronto as well have had some benefit. Therefore, we are really discussing this piece of legislation as relating to an emergency situation, without really having been informed about the scope of the emergency.
I am sure that the port of Montreal over the past 50 or 75 years, and until the last three or four years, has always experienced some difficulty because for a period of five or six months in the year the river was frozen. When several new icebreakers were commissioned a few years ago the situation was obviously changed considerably for the port of Montreal. I believe there have been difficulties at the port of Montreal previously which did not have a national consequence, even though the port was totally closed for periods of four or five months in the year.
The point I am making is that we are being asked to pass national legislation to end a situation with which I, personally, am not too familiar and which the minister himself has not outlined. I do not know whether a bushel of grain has been delayed because of the strike. I took it upon myself, in order to obtain information, to make several phone calls to people I know who are very close to the port in Montreal. I asked them whether the port was closed and how many ships were in the port. They said the port is not closed and is operating as usual. They indicated something the minister has not mentioned. There really are four or five major unions operating in the port of Montreal, loading, unloading and handling cargo in that area. They include the CBRT, the CNTU, the Mercantile
25319-56J

July 6, 1972
St. Lawrence Ports Operations Bill
Union, the Longshoremen's Union and I presume other unions associated with other aspects of moving cargo on the dock.
The port of Montreal I am sure has built up over a period of years, and now on a year-around basis, a very large mercantile trade. It has done so in the import-export field and more recently in the container field. I am sure any disruption in this traffic would have an effect on the community, on the people who work in the dock area and, in faction the economy of Montreal in general. Whether or not this has reached the disaster level that would warrant this type of emergency legislation I am not sure. I suggest that no one, including the newspapers and other media which usually are fairly diligent in searching out information that would enable Members of Parliament to make a fairly good decision in respect of the emergency, has been diligent in investigating the rumour that grain is not being shipped as a result of the stevedores' strike. I spoke to some people who work as crew members on ships in the Great Lakes and the St. Lawrence Seaway, and they tell me there has not been one of their ships which has suffered any difficulty. There have been changes in places of loading and unloading, the destinations have been changed and other changes have taken place, but there has been no dislocation.
The point I am making is that I am not opposed to us doing something about the situation, but I am of the opinion that we are not dealing with a national emergency in even a very small sense. It may be that this has developed into that type of a problem, but if that is so, I am not aware of it. I have been involved in many strikes and I can assure you that if a large number of people are unemployed for eight weeks they Eire in serious difficulty. I am sure that if there are others on the management side who are operating businesses, and who are not having their deliveries made to their home port, they are also having difficulties. But I think that this bill contains no provisions that will solve the problems which originally caused this strike and, in fact, the decision on those points is now being left to an arbitrator who is to make a settlement some time in the future.
I suggest it is unfortunate that we did not have available to us the section of the new Labour Code under which a mediator could have been appointed to represent the public before a situation hardened to the extent that a compromise was no longer possible. I disagree with the minister. There is no question about his sincerity, honesty or integrity, but I think that he was overly cautious in not entering this dispute three or four weeks ago. Obviously, the problem did not appear to be any closer to settlement no matter whom he sent to negotiate on his behalf, and it seems to me that the minister had an opportunity to settle the dispute earlier.
This legislation would not be before us today if the former minister of labour had been the minister, because I am sure he would have gone to the parties and said: "I demand on behalf of the nation that this matter be settled. I will assist you to settle it and I will stay here until it is settled". Many of us can remember much more serious situations than this one when the minister went to Montreal and stayed there for several days at great personal

sacrifice to his health and to his personsd wellbeing. However, the parties did arrive at a settlement because no matter what the problem is only two people can arrive at the settlement and those two people represent management on the one hand, and the workers on the other. Until those two people decide to reach a decision, there will not be a decision. Unless the workers in this case decide that that can be accomplished with the arbitrator acting in the role of a trustee, there really is no reason for them to go back to work and they are not likely to do so. We will not, therefore, be much closer to reaching a solution than we have been in the past.
I do not believe it is fair to Members of Parliament and to the country for us to pass this legislation as emergency legislation. So far as labour relations Eire concerned, this is a very drastic type of legislation. The government has involved itself in this dispute and they will arrive at a settlement. I congratulate the minister for having introduced what is probably the mildest form of government intervention that he could find, and I sincerely hope that the arbitrator will be able to act on behalf of both parties in the role of a trustee. He will certainly have to have the patience and the ability of Solomon to arrive at a conclusion of a problem which involves technical changes entailing a smaller work force in the future. Therefore, his job will not be an easy one and a solution will not be found easily. I suggest that one of the weaknesses in passing legislation of this nature is that we are not able to ceiII witnesses.

Mr. Chairman, I am getting considerable help and it seems that the committee of the whole now resembles a standing committee with witnesses before it. Of course, the witnesses are not reliable because obviously they have an interest in the subject, and we should really face the problem on that basis. But I did want to say that this is a very serious step that Parliament is
July 6, 1972

taking. I hope that the results of the legislation will prove we were right in taking this step. I sincerely hope that the minister's wish is that in the future the appointment of a mediator will represent a totally new force in labour relations and that the interest of the general public can be served by the introduction of a mediator under the Labour Code at a very early stage of future negotiations. The minister said quite rightly that we should not be making the decision as to the final outcome of this conflict because the facts are so complicated that the mediator who had been appointed by the government was unable to make recommendations, and that therefore we should leave that area wide open. With that I agree, Mr. Chairman, but I do suggest that we are taking a very serious step on only hearsay information.
I would have been much happier with this bill if the minister had outlined not only the difficulty that developed in the labour dispute, which I can comprehend from reading the previous contract and looking at the changes made in the recent contract as well as the recommendations made by those who looked at the recent contract, but had also outlined in more detail the effect on the public interest. If this bill had been introduced in the normal course of a parliamentary session rather than in its dying days, we would never have given consideration to it without considerably more information. I sincerely hope that the judgment made by government members, when deciding to present this legislation, is justified. I sincerely hope that passage of the bill will go some way towards ending a problem that not only involves this union but will involve other unions, as was the case several years ago with the Freedman report on the reduction of railway crews and the retirement of people made supernumerary because of technical changes in industry.
I hope, Mr. Chairman, that the desired results will be achieved, and that parliament in future, before this kind of decision is made, will be given much more information. We are not here to negotiate contracts between management and unions. We are meeting in an emergency situation to solve a problem that has become detrimental to a large segment of the Canadian population. On that side of the problem, we have received very little information that is not hearsay. Investigations made by hon. members have not been sufficient to date, and therefore reliance on the government is necessary. I hope this bill carries with it a sense of responsibility on the part of the government, and that this action will be sufficient to eliminate the problem.

Mr. Chairman, the object of the sanctions in the bill is to make it as effective as possible. In this instance, in my judgment the most effective sanction with respect to the longshore unions is to proceed through their officials. In this specific instance it has been the wilful acts of officers of this union that have led to the situation in which we now find ourselves.
I address myself to another aspect of the question raised by the hon. member to point out that under the present laws, under the Canada Labour Code, a union as such can be proceeded against for any violation of a labour agreement or the Canada Labour Code. For those purposes there is no question that a union is a corporate person, is a person under the law. We know that in civil proceedings a union can be proceeded against in the courts by way of injunction and by way of contempt proceedings. Yesterday a judgment was rendered which levied fines for contempt of a court order, not only on the union but on individual officers. Therefore, part of the answer to the question is that under the Canada Labour Code, or under civil proceedings, the union may be proceeded against as such.
What we are discussing here, and what we have in front of us is a specific bill, an emergency bill, in which penalties are not specifically spelled out; the penalties are those which flow through the Criminal Code of Canada. In my judgment this would be most effective in bringing about the results we want. The results we want are surely not extremely punitive ones, but to get the men back to work and to get the ports operating. To do that, in my judgment, and I hope that members of the House will support me in this, the most effective way of proceeding is through the officers of the union, as the bill provides.

Mr. Chairman, I understand we are discussing clause 2 of the bill. Clause 2 defines "strike" in part as:
-a cessation of work or a refusal to work or to continue to work by employees,-
There are a few other words which I do not need to mention. By reason of this definition, the effect of this bill will be to limit the right of a person to strike, to cease working, to refuse to work or to refuse to continue to work. I support this clause with extreme reluctance. I was happy to note that the minister also expressed extreme reluctance over it. I believe, and my associations in the past with the trade union movement may be partly responsible for my views, that the right to strike is absolutely essential if we are to maintain an industrial democracy. I think that there should be an order directing people back to work only in cases of clear, national emergency.
I differ with my colleague for Timiskaming here. There is no doubt that this strike lasting eight weeks in those important ports does constitute a national emergency and this legislation is therefore justified, but only, in my view, because there is such a national emergency. When three of our main ports to a large extent have been closed down, when the entire wheat industry which maintains the Prairies and which is an important factor in the economic well being of our country is threatened because farmers are not able to distribute their produce as a result of this strike, I say the time has come to act, although I accept this action with great reluctance. I hope this bill will receive the unanimous support of this House, because I believe it represents the will of the people of Canada.

Mr. Chairman, in my remarks on second reading yesterday, I drew attention to what I believe to be a shortcoming in this clause. I was hoping the minister might come forward with an amendment which would overcome what I believe would be a serious difficulty.
I have not asked any questions, nor, as I recall it, have any of my hon. friends, about sanctions and the like because I think it is obvious that if the law which Parliament is seeking to establish by this bill is disregarded and

July 6, 1972
St. Lawrence Ports Operations Bill
we are placed in the position of having to think of sanctions, the exercise we are now undertaking will have failed. I join the minister in hoping that everyone concerned will obey this law as being the will not only of parliament but of the people of Canada. From my conversations by telephone with some people in Montreal I have great ground for hope that the law will be obeyed, at least on the labour side, and I have no reason to doubt that it will be obeyed on the management side. Obviously, when one is dealing with a large number of people-some 3,000 individual members-it is impossible to say how each one of them will act. But I am not so much concerned about sanctions, whether they are included in this bill or whether those contained in the Criminal Code will apply. I take this position because I hope, as I am sure does everyone in this House, that sanctions will not be required. As a matter of fact, the sanctions in the Criminal Code are probably more severe than any which the minister would probably have placed in this bill had he thought it necessary to move along those lines.
Unlike the hon. member for Trinity I am one Member of Parliament who appreciates deeply the approach which the minister and the government have taken. I do not hesitate to express my appreciation when I believe it to be deserved. I appreciate deeply the approach which the minister and the government have taken in this case, seeking to end this dispute and to get the industry rolling again rather than to produce a punitive piece of legislation.
It is within this framework that I believe the minister has proposed, in 7(2)(b), to give the arbitrator what appear to me to be powers wider than are appropriate in the circumstances. I understand the point which is worrying the minister and everyone concerned. I know a little-not very much-about the workings of these ports. I know, for example, that they are busy in May and June, relatively slow in July and August and the early part of September, and become busy again in September, October and November. What has happened is that the failure to deal with any tonnage during what would normally have been the busy months of the year, May and June, has meant that no funds, or only a very small fund, is now available from which to discharge the guarantee of 40 hours per week and 37 weeks work per year for which, as I understand it, the job security plan under the collective agreement provides. I can well understand that it should be necessary to allow for a period of time, whatever that period may be, during which funds might be collected and placed in the kitty, before the job security plan becomes effective. For this reason I have no hesitation about accepting section 7(2)(a) which gives the arbitrator the right not only to fix the date but to make those modifications which Eire necessary in reference to the date of the application of the job security plan.
However, it seems to me, and I should like to hear the minister on this point, that it is a serious error to give the arbitrator authority, as is done in 7(2)(b), to make changes in the entire plan even beyond the year 1972. I am not thinking about the unions, now, because the unions are not affected. It is the pocketbooks of the union members that are affected and this provision opens the door to serious and valid objection on the part of union members.
I must say, frankly, that if I were a longshoreman and a

member of one of these unions I would be very much upset by the proposition advanced in this clause, even if I were the most reasonable longshoreman-and obviously, Mr. Chairman, if I were one I would be reasonable. That goes without question.

subtopic: ST. LAWRENCE PORTS OPERATIONS BILL MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR RESUMPTION OF LONGSHORING AND RELATED OPERATIONS
speechtext: Don't flatter yourself.

subtopic: ST. LAWRENCE PORTS OPERATIONS BILL MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR RESUMPTION OF LONGSHORING AND RELATED OPERATIONS
speechtext:
I would accept the proposal that the arbitrator be given the right to set a date in 1972 when the plan was to apply, but I would feel that my rights were really in danger if the arbitrator were also given the right to modify the plan, as is done in the paragraph to which I have referred. The paragraph reads:
making such modifications to those plans and those provisions as in his opinion are required to give effect thereto on and after the date fixed by him.
The minister said yesterday, I gather, that these words were in some way confining. Perhaps I misunderstood him. I do not find them confining at all. The words are confined to the job security plan, but there is no limit placed on the modifications the arbitrator is empowered to make. There is apparently no limit on his authority to make changes in the plan. I ask the minister to give serious attention to this submission. I am prepared, if necessary, to move an amendment, but our proceedings have gone fairly fast this afternoon and I believe we have a few minutes in which to exchange views. I take the hon. gentleman back to his own statement, one which I not only accept but support, that he is not interested in anything punitive but only in getting these ports rolling.
I say that this paragraph contains an unjustifiable provision aimed not at the unions or something abstract, but at the livelihood of the longshoremen in the two remaining years of this agreement, 1973 and 1974. That kind of provision is provocative. I know the minister did not intend that, do not misunderstand me. I have the greatest respect for the very honourable way in which he has approached this problem, even though I had criticisms about the timing of his intervention. I know he does not intend to provoke them, but I tell him not only from logic but, if I may say so, from some conversations I have had that this clause is provocative and threatening to the longshoremen. I say it is not necessary.
As I said yesterday, the succeeding clause, Clause 8, gives the minister the authority to appoint an arbitrator to deal with any dispute that may arise. I am paraphrasing his statement. If it becomes necessary in January, February or March of 1973, because things develop in such a way the employer has not got enough funds to live up to the agreement and the unions say that he must, the minister would then have the opportunity to say to the unions and the company they must take this matter to arbitration. If they refuse to do so, then he would be able to do it.

I do not see any doubt arising. The other point I should like to come to is that the authority of the arbitrator is to make a judgment at some point in time. Let us say sometime in the future or in the fall, for the sake of argument, he will make that judgment. At that time, he will fix a date. At that time also, he will be considering the modifications which in his judgment are required, and only those modifications as are required to give effect to the job security plan in the altered circumstances that the work stoppage has brought about. I believe the hon. member for York South would agree with me that the arbitrator has that single opportunity. It is not a recurring opportunity to make awards with regard to the job security plan down through 1972,1973 and 1974.

St. Lawrence Ports Operations Bill
The arbitrator has an obligation under this legislation to consider all the facts and make his award at a given point in time when he feels he is in possession of sufficient facts to know how the job security plan, particularly the funding operation, is working in view of the operations of the port. At that point, he will make his judgment in respect of any modification he deems necessary. I do not know whether there is any doubt in the mind of anyone concerning whether that is his point in time.
Again on the third point, it seems to me inappropriate to state now in this bill that when the arbitrator comes to making those modifications, being in possession of facts which we are not in possession of now, and having behind him some experience concerning the operations as they resume, he should be confined to December 31, 1972 in respect of those modifications. It might be his opinion that this delay ought to continue until March, April or the end of the first year of the agreement, or something else. He might find in his judgment, looking at the facts, that the putting of a date in the bill would be an obstacle to his making the job security provisions the viable instrument they are intended to be under the collective agreement. That is the reason we have not thought it appropriate to specify a date such as the end of this year.
I think I would be on good ground in going on to say- and I do not want to presume upon the role of the arbitrator-that in all likelihood any modification he is likely to deem necessary should, in fact, not be prolonged beyond the end of the year. The funding arrangements, as I understand them, are on an annual basis, but be that as it may, he is the one in possession of the facts and it is his judgment. I would not want these latter remarks I have just concluded to enter into his judgment when the time comes. I do say that as we stand here today expecting the ports to resume their operations, knowing that a busy season is still in front of the ports of Montreal, Quebec and Trois-Rivieres, it would be our hope that modifications would be as limited as they can be in time. I think that is what the hon. member for York South is really getting at. The duration of the modifications should be as limited as feasible.
I think in this matter we are entitled to have some confidence in the judicious decisions of the arbitrator as named in the agreement. He has a thorough understanding of the operations of the port, a thorough understanding of the collective agreements and a thorough understanding of the intentions of the parties, having been their permanent arbitrator for a number of years. He has also been the chairman of the conciliation board which assisted in the production of this particular agreement. He knows the history of the port and is familiar with its operations. In addition, he knows the parties concerned. In view of all this, I think we can have confidence in the judgment he would render and in his ability to make a judicious decision.
There is one further point in respect of the possible bearing on clause 7 of clause 8. The hon. member for York South raised the possibility that the minister, if neither of the two parties took action, might under clause 8 put into operation a regulation which would involve the possibility of modifying the job security plan at some future time after the arbitrator had made the ruling which we expect 
him to make under this legislation. I cannot read into clause 8 any such possibility. I doubt that the words can be stretched to mean that. That clause is there to cope with the normal exercise of an arbitrator's role under the collective agreement as it continues down to its termination three years hence-that is to say, the interpretation of matters which arise, and the settlement in a final way of disagreements which arise over alleged violations, and so on. It would not, in my view, extend the arbitrator's power to modify the agreement in any way but only to continue to interpret it. The experience we have had up until now is that at one stage neither party was willing to initiate this arbitration procedure. In light of that experience, this clause would give the minister the extra leverage of initiating a normal type of arbitration proceeding if once again neither party appeared willing to so initiate. I would not expect that circumstance to arise, but it did seem wise to incorporate clause 8 in the event that it might arise.

Mr. Chairman, I wish with all my heart that I could accept the minister's position, but I cannot. I think he has been in this dispute long enough to learn about longshoring perhaps more than I know, but I know enough about it to know that for many years this particular occupation was so uncertain, the job security was so lacking, that for many decades it attracted the transient type of worker who was available on the docks for a month and then disappeared. Someone else might be available for a week or for a season, and then disappear.
Not so many years ago the turnover of workers in the longshoring occupation was so high that every stevedoring company I met during some years of association with this industry would even then-and that was in the middle and late 1950's-complain about the fact that they could not have a secure and steady work force that knew what was happening, that was committed to the job and had loyalty to the work and to the employer. For all the years that I have known the situation, longshoremen have been fighting like hell-if you will permit me to speak plain English-to obtain some kind of job security in their work. As many of them said to me when I was associated with them in Hamilton and Toronto, they wanted job security so that those of them who wanted to do so could make the occupation of stevedoring a lifelong occupation, which they could not do if they could not be sure of having more than so many weeks of work a year. At that time the employer had the right to say whom he would or would not call, and how many days or weeks of work there were during which a longshoreman would be employed.
So, they have fought very hard for years, and this particular problem in Montreal is not the first one that has arisen out of job security arguments. Finally, they arrived at a collective agreement in April of this year which contains a job security program. What the minister is proposing in this legislation is that the whole of the job security program can be fiddled with by the arbitrator, every aspect of it, and the job security program is at the basis of the whole problem. The minister says-I am sure with utmost honesty-that this clause confines the arbitrator's powers solely to the area of the job security plan. Of course it does, but it happens to be at the heart of the matter. Giving someone an opportunity to pierce your heart, and limiting him to doing only that, will not help the minister's life. A pierced heart is enough to do all the
St. Lawrence Ports Operations Bill
damage that he could possibly tolerate, and the job security program is at the heart of this collective agreement, at the heart of the relationship between the longshoremen and their employers in these ports, as it is in other ports. Therefore, what the minister is suggesting and insisting upon is that the arbitrator have the authority to change any aspect of the plan. There is nothing in the clause which prevents him from saying that instead of a guaranteed 40 hours a week it should be 35 hours a week. Instead of guaranteeing 37 weeks, he could guarantee only 30. He could do that with the powers given to him in this clause.
The minister says he has confidence the arbitrator will do the right thing. I am not throwing any doubt on that confidence. I do not know who the arbitrator will be. Unfortunately I suspect, although I hope I am wrong, that the fact this blessed hassle has gone on, and that Judge Gold has already been used and brought down an award that the unions have rejected, will mean the creation of a difficult situation. I understand that Judge Gold, whom I do not know, whom I have never had the pleasure of meeting or appearing before, is a really great chap who knows this area, knows the port and stevedoring operations, has a great deal of integrity, and a real concern for the situation, just as we have in this chamber. But that will not solve the problem. When you say to a worker or any ordinary person, "You can rely on this man," that does not satisfy him. You could not persuade me, if I were a longshoreman, that I need not worry about the fact that the arbitrator will have all the power necessary to break the basis of my job security. Even if you say to me, "Don't worry, he is a good guy; he is only going to amputate one of your legs not both your legs," I will still worry.
Yet this is the kind of thing the minister is placing before employees whom he is asking to go back to work. He is saying that the very basis of the collective agreement, the very basis of their livelihood, about which they thought they had some guarantee in the collective agreement, is now open to an arbitrator to destroy or to reduce to any extent he likes. I think the minister is unwise in doing that. I have the fullest confidence in his good intentions, but I do not have to remind him of a rather banal road that is paved with good intentions.
Let me make another suggestion to the minister. I am really doing my darndest to persuade him to do this, not only to protect the livelihood of the stevedores which I make no apology for trying to do, but also to make sure that the bill will have the best possible chance of doing the job he wants done. I hope he will take a few more minutes to think about limiting the arbitrator's power to modify just until the end of 1972, and give himself, as Minister of Labour, authority to modify the situation further if either side, management or union, ask him to do so because of complaints they have, or fears they have that the plan will not work. If he would consider some such approach, the workers could go back to work in the knowledge that their job security plan will not be interfered with beyond 1972, at least so far as the arbitrator is concerned. If the minister is worried about what might happen next year if there is not enough money in the fund, and I notice that according to the agreement a certain amount, $21 million, has to be there for 1973-74, he should give himself the

July 6, 1972
St. Lawrence Ports Operations Bill
power, on the application of either the employers or the union, to appoint an arbitrator to modify the plan further for 1973 if that becomes necessary.
I am not interested in taking credit for moving an amendment, but I suggest common sense should caution the minister to move year by year. The minister says that an arbitrator sitting in September or October will have the facts before him. He won't, Mr. Chairman. He will not know what the shipping situation will be next spring. From long experience, I assure the minister that the Maritime Employers Association will come before the arbitrator with graphs, facts and figures to show that next year is not going to be good year. They will attempt to show that the agreement they arrived at last April is too rich for their blood, and they will present facts and figures to project what will happen next year. It is that kind of argument which the union and the employees will resent.
The minister would be better off to retain this power to appoint an arbitrator again in 1973 if the association, or a member of it tells him, "I cannot carry out my job security arrangements; will you please appoint someone under the authority you have, so that I can present my case to him." It should not take the minister's advisers more than 15 minutes to draft such an amendment. I plead with him that it is unjust to go to the workers in Montreal, Trois-Rivieres and Quebec City and tell them, "Go back to work; I have given an arbitrator total authority to fiddle with the entire job security plan that you adopted last April." There is great danger in that approach.

I am sorry to be badgering both the minister and the members of the committee, Mr. Chairman. Let me say, first of all, that the minister and his advisers certainly misunderstood me when they thought my suggestion that he give himself power to appoint an arbitrator at any time, next year or the year after, meant that he would have to make a decision on whether there was a case for appointing an arbitrator. I did not intend that, and I am not going to make a long speech because obviously if the minister does not agree, that is the end of it. I intended that such provision would be automatic. When one of the parties requested him to appoint an arbitrator he would do so, and the case would be in the hands of the arbitrator rather than in the hands of the minister.
Mr. Chairman, I just cannot buy the minister's reaction of equanimity to this proposition. He says that the arbitrator will make those modifications that are needed, and only to the extent required. I say to the minister those are just words. All the time that I am arguing here, figuratively I am sitting in the hall where the longshoremen meet in Montreal. As a longshoreman, when this bill is read to me and when the minister or somebody else tells me that the arbitrator is going to do it only to the extent required, I ask myself and I ask him what in Heaven's name is the extent required? He cannot satisfy me by using those general, syrupy words. What is involved is not something abstract. What is involved is my job security next year. What is involved is the question of whether or not I will get paid 40 hours a week for 37 weeks in 1973, and 40 hours a week for 37 weeks in 1974. That is what is involved for me, as a longshoreman, not some abstract
St. Lawrence Ports Operations Bill
query. When you say to me I should accept this law, I will, as a law abiding citizen, accept it; but, let me tell you, I am good and mad because you are giving this arbitrator this kind of power. Do not come back to me again; I am not going to listen to you, because you are selling me down the river. It may be that you are right, and the arbitrator will do me justice; but you cannot guarantee that. I do not know how much he will listen to my employer or how much he will listen to me.
These are practical considerations which anybody who has been in any way involved with the ranks of the working people knows enter the heads of working people. This, after all, is important to the worker's life, to his future and to the future of his family next year and the year after. You cannot persuade me that this arbitrator needs any more power than to set a date and to make modifications for the year 1972. And, if I am an objective longshoreman, I will have to admit that my being out on strike for eight weeks has destroyed the job security plan for this year.
I do not suppose I am getting anywhere with the minister, Mr. Chairman. Let me say this to him, as if I were speaking still as a member of the work force: Last April my union made a collective agreement with management for that job security plan. Last year management did not know exactly where the money was to come from; they do not know where it is to come from this year, let alone next year. Why are you giving anybody the authority to deny me any part of the job security plan in 1973?

AGRICULTURE
subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR COPY OF REPORT ON UNITED STATES INTERNAL FOOD-AID PROGRAM
speechtext:
That an Order of the House do issue for a copy of the report undertaken in the Department of Agriculture on the United States Internal Food-Aid Program and its application to Canada.
She said: Mr. Speaker, as my party's House leader suggested, I would have been perfectly happy, in view of the serious nature of the legislation before the House this afternoon, to forgo my opportunity to participate in private members' hour. I am sorry, for my part, that in these circumstances we are proceeding with private members' hour. However, that is what the House has decided, and we must go along with that decision.
My notice of motion for the production of papers refers to something I have wanted to obtain for some time, a copy of the report or study undertaken in the Department of Agriculture with regard to the United States internal food-aid program and its application to Canada. A number of similar requests have been made and refused. I made a request last week which was refused. I suppose

the government, in its own mind, can make a case for not releasing documents which might cause trouble for members of the government or others if they were released. However, I cannot for the life of me see that there could be any such objection to this report being released. Certainly, it has nothing to do with internal security. I cannot see how it could affect our relations with the United States.
The documents in question merely have to do with the reaction of the Canadian Department of Agriculture to the internal food-aid program of the United States. I think our great neighbour to the south may be flattered to learn that we are looking at what it is doing in supplementing the diet of low income people. I cannot understand why this report should not be made available to us, unless of course, the government does not like the nature of the report that officials of the Department of Agriculture have made. It may well be the report indicates that a government program ought to be set up for distributing food to low income groups in this country who, because of their poverty, are genuinely undernourished. It may be that there are things in the report the government did not wish to make public, in view of possible public reaction. Frankly, I do not see how anybody's nose could be put out of joint if the report were made available to us. It would not hurt the officials concerned or the government.
There is another possible reason behind the refusal. Possibly this report is not being released because of this government's deplorable tendency to secrecy. It wants to hide all such reports which have been compiled simply because taxpayers' money was available for compiling them. The taxpayers of this country have spent much money on studies, on committee reports, reports of commissions, and all the rest of it. When the government gets these reports, either because it is not inclined to do anything about them or because it is afraid of the reaction of the public if the facts were made known and the government did not act on them or because it is arrogant to the point that it wants to keep these reports as its private property, it refuses to allow the public to get the facts. This is a completely indefensible attitude. This government sits on these reports so long that, after a while there are leaks from one place or another, whether natural or inspired I do not know, and this indicates that the policy does not sit well with the public.
I want to emphasize that the taxpayers have a right to see the results of this report. We, the representatives of the people, also have a right to see the report. Just this afternoon, questions were asked about a report on housing. This whole field badly needs attention. The government has had a whole flock of reports on this situation. We know that the translations of many of them have been prepared. By what right does the government hold these and keep them under wraps? It is simply because they have more members and a greater club. That is wrong. If we cannot do anything else in this House except get rid of the secrecy surrounding the production of reports which are paid for by the taxpayers of this country, we will have done something good. Why do we have Information Canada? Information Canada releases only things which the government wants released. They stand solid and do
July 6, 1972

not yield anything that the taxpayers should have in order that their elected representatives can make judgments.
I now come to the report. The worst of it is that we do not know what is in it and we have no means of telling. We do know that the Department of Agriculture has made a study of the United States internal food-aid program and its application to Canada, but we have no evidence as to what is in the report. The United States has made efforts to get food to low income groups by the food stamp plan and other plans. This government has not lifted one finger to get food to the low income groups who need it. If the government has made a study of the United States internal food program, it would be highly desirable for the public to know what our great neighbour to the south has been doing and what the officials of the Department of Agriculture think about it.
I wish to quote from an article in the June 15 edition of the Globe and Mail:
-the U.S. Department of Agriculture has thousands of "nutrition aides" who give basic nutritional advice to mothers; it prints and distributes literature on the subject; a few school systems and universities provide some training in nutrition. But most do nothing. And nowhere, to my knowledge, is there a co-ordinated approach to teaching the subject of nutrition.
The United States has not gone too far in that direction, but it has at least reached the stage of having thousands of nutrition aides. What is a nutrition aide? Presumably it is a young person, not a college graduate, but one who can grasp the basic essentials of nutrition and can indicate where literature, officers and information can be found. If this government was looking at ways and means of providing jobs for young people, it could hire nutrition aides. We have nurses aides and teaching aides. Hopefully, if there is another government in power, we will one day have day care centre aids. This government does not have the stamina or willpower to open these. The United States has at least created the position of nutrition aide.
We know that Canada's low income groups need help in getting a proper diet. Let no one tell me that there is poor nutrition in all groups. I know that. However, the difference between poor nutrition in upper income and low income families is very great. Those in the upper income groups can read and study what is nutritionally advisable if they wish. No matter how those in the low income group study and read, they cannot have a better diet because they do not have the financial resources.
At the risk of boring some members, and I find some are easily bored when it comes to problems affecting the family in this country, I want to refer to a very important editorial that appeared in a recent edition of the Globe and Mail. This is an article about a remarkable woman, Agnes Higgins, the director of the Montreal Diet Dispensary. For years she has been conducting research into diet deficiencies in low income groups who require social assistance. I and other members in this House have been quoting the findings of Mrs. Higgins for a long time. Mrs. Higgins has now made an important study about the nutritional needs of Canadians. I will not go over all the knowledge on which this is based, but this report of Mrs. Higgins and her colleagues on their Montreal experiment was one of five nutrition papers chosen for presentation to the International Congress of Endocrinology in Washington. That is what the world thinks of Mrs. Higgins,
U.S. Internal Food-Aid Program
even though Canadians have not been fortunate enough to know her studies exist because of the failure of this government to inform them. I quote:
Mrs. Higgins based her work on the research of others which had proved, among other things: that it was risky to the baby to try to keep the mother's weight during pregnancy fashionably down; that mothers who were well nourished during the last 15 weeks of their pregnancies produced bigger babies; that bigger babies (7 to 81 pounds are considered the best weights) tend to have more brain cells than smaller babies; that small babies have drastically increased rates of stillbirths, deaths in the first weeks and months of life, cerebral palsy, mental retardation and lowered intelligence.
Functioning from this knowledge Mrs. Higgins and her colleagues went to work on some of the most deprived mothers in Canada, women from two public clinics in poverty-stricken areas of Montreal.
Between 1963 and 1971 their study group included 1,725 mothers. Of these, 1,055 had five years of education or less, 1,164 were so poor that they were entitled to food supplements, 515 of the pregnancies were illegitimate. Not a promising group, one would have thought; yet only 5 per cent dropped out of the course.
On her first visit to the clinic each mother was assessed on the basis of income and diet. If her income was large enough, she was told what she should eat and given a standard mineral and vitamin supplement.
If her income was too small-and the incomes of 67 per cent of the mothers were too small-she was given food supplements of milk, eggs, oranges and the standard minerals and vitamins. Her needs were carefully calculated to take into consideration underweight, protein deficiency, shortage of calories and special conditions of stress.
All mothers were visited at least once in their homes.
They received the same medical attention.
The average birthweight for these babies was the same as for babies born to private patients at these hospitals. The record with respect to premature births and early death was as good as that for private patients, and significantly better than for other public clinic cases who had not had the diet treatment, and significantly better than the Canadian average.
Now, I come to the part which I hope will touch the cockles of the hearts of even the hardened people who make all their judgments on the basis of how much it costs or how little it costs or how much they can get away with.
A single family can perhaps most graphically paint the picture. A 29-year-old mother had borne 11 children. The first eight were born without diet assistance, and all had small birth weights. One died at the age of one month. For her last three pregnancies the mother had diet assistance, and these three babies all weighed within the ideal range.
A physical and mental assessment of all the children was done at Montreal Children's Hospital. The last three children were found to be normal. All of the others were found to be disadvantaged and likely to require support off and on through life.
Now, I get to the nub of the thing.
It cost the public $125 to give the mother diet assistance, including the free milk, oranges, eggs and vitamins, for each of her normal babies. The cost to the public of maintaining a defective child throughout life in an institution or in the community is more than $100,000.
So, there you have it in terms of actual cost-$125 to produce a healthy baby and $100,000 to keep a defective child in an institution for life. It would pay us a thousand times over in dollars and cents to apply Mrs. Higgins' good sense and compassion whenever circumstances call

July 6, 1972
U.S. Internal Food-Aid. Program
for it. This is why I want that report. I want to see whether there is anything in it which would supply further evidence of the need to supplement the diets of poor people, people living on social assistance and low incomes. It is no use saying we should wait until the results of the nutrition survey are known. The report will not be completed until this fall, and the best we can hope for is that it will be available next spring. Next spring we shall be told we cannot have it because hon. members on the other side are sitting on it. Why wait for spring? Do it now! Let us begin right away to learn all we can from what our neighbours in the United States have done. Let us get ahead on the basis of what we can learn; let us get going right away and supplement the diets of the people in this country who most need assistance.

subtopic: AGRICULTURE
subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR COPY OF REPORT ON UNITED STATES INTERNAL FOOD-AID PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to thank the hon. member for Vaneouver-Kingsway (Mrs. Maclnnis) for her work in explaining to us the situation and also for giving us the opportunity of talking about the feeding habits in Canada.
Some may have bad eating habits, even if they have a rather high income. It is not the income of a person which gives him good eating habits, but mainly the way the mother buys the foods and prepares them for the family.
In my capacity of chairman of school boards for many years, I had the opportunity of surveying the eating habits of large families, particularly children attending school, and I am convinced that Canada is a rich country from the standpoint of foodstuffs; we are mainly producers able to supply adequate food to Canadians.
One can spend $50 a week feeding a family of four or five children and even then not eat properly. Indeed, one can buy all sorts of things like hot dogs, as was pointed out earlier, and live on hamburgers just as well as abundant farm products.
Undernourishment should be studied because in Canada, as I said before, people suffer from it, not for lack of money but for lack of selecting the proper foods to be eaten. I have studied some family budgets. In fact, after a discussion with a housewife who told me, to my astonishment, that she fed her five children and her husband on $50 a week, my first reaction was to wonder if my wife managed my budget properly because I know how much it costs to feed my family.
Evidently, when we have the means to buy products of the highest quality or some luxury goods, we can spend more for food, but it does not necessarily mean that we are better fed. If we closely consider the problem, we realize, for example, that we have not yet reached the point where it is urgent to carry out the American program in Canada.
If on the other hand it has been deemed necessary to study what was going on in the neighbouring countries to determine whether the food aid programs were better than ours, we necessarily had to turn toward the United States to get information on food.
Apparently, under a certain program, the people can buy food in groceries with coupons. Customers cannot exchange these vouchers for money because this is forbidden. If it should happen that the value of their vouchers

exceed the value of their purchases, the retailer would be required to deliver some kind of receipt that they could use again.
The system, which was established by legislation passed in the United States in 1964 and amended on a few occasions, and particularly in January 1971, costs the American Treasury $2 billion and perhaps today more than $3 billion.
Of course, when you distribute the cost among 200 million citizens, you do not reach a fantastic sum per capita, but when you want to apply this system in this country, you have to multiply this figure by 10. We then find out that for a food program similar to the American effort we would have to spend more than $250 million. Therefore, if the federal government had to make such an amount available, over and above what it already pays through cost-sharing programs and other social measures, we see readily that astronomic amounts would burden the budget of assistance to underprivileged persons.
It must be realized that Canadians engaged in food production far outnumber those in the United States. We must also realize that the American economy can support measures that we could not add to those already in force. Their effects on the sales of food must also be assessed. What would happen if the people that we are now assisting through social measures benefited from increased assistance under a coupon distribution program?
These are effects that we should consider beCause of their short, middle and long term bearing. However, I am interested in one aspect of the American program: in Canada we grant direct benefits to the needy through social measures. Considering their skills I sometimes wonder if they properly use the money given to them.
Would a coupon system or something else which would compel them to allot part of their budget to food not be preferable to the present system? It is a question which deserves consideration and further study. We are not now in a position to take such a quick decision on a program which could entail large federal expenditures.
Mr. Speaker, there is another point that should perhaps be considered. Some may think it is rather sophisticated, but a family food-aid program might be conducive to serious abuses. Very often, when money is not available in some families, the coupons distributed under all kinds of forms could be exchanged for money which could be applied to other purposes.
In Canada and in the United States there are quantities of foods rich in protein, such as eggs, poultry, etc. For the last twenty years, the price of these foods have declined sharply. Low income families consume much of these foods. One cannot say that in Canada it is impossible to find protein-rich foods at reasonable prices.
Mr. Speaker, I would now like to talk about another aspect. I would like first to indicate that I am not at all opposed, to having now and in the future as many studies and surveys as possible on our national diet. We will have to deal with this problem sometime, hopefully with a great deal of care and attention. I am convinced that there might be a distribution of food in Canada. However, the
July 6, 1972

main problem remains the economic situation of producers. In cases of overproduction, producers are seldom in a position to break even. Insofar as producers are concerned, the distribution of surplus foods products in the homes will not actually resolve economic problems. Surpluses are shipped to another area. A tremendous effort could be made so that producers may be in a better situation and that they may earn at least a decent living which will enable them through taxes to contribute to other programs intended for poor or low income people.
We must export our food surplus. I would be remiss in my duty if I did not comment on the assistance which Canada is extending to developing countries. We are still not doing all we could and should in this field.
I do not think Mr. Speaker, that French Canadians have to eat like the Americans and conduct surveys, in view of the fact that they are in a position to eat with the commodities at their disposal.
In fact, Mr. Speaker, there is no scarcity of food in Canada. We know that all food and agricultural areas in Canada are showing huge production surpluses. We know also that every farmer and industry which is involved in food production only wish to have more consumers buying their products.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I begin by complimenting the hon. member who has just concluded his speech. I assume from the interest he has shown in this debate that he is in favour of the production of papers in respect of the internal food-aid program which for a number of years has been carried on in the United States. I wish, also, to compliment the hon. member for Vancouv-er-Kingsway (Mrs. Maclnnis) for her excellent outline of some of the difficulties surrounding nutrition in the Canadian setting. I hesitated to take part in this debate because I have no experience of pregnancy; therefore I shall confine my remarks strictly to questions of food, food consumption and nutrition.
The hon. member on the other side of the House pointed out that a program such as that being carried on in the United States jvould cost $250 million to implement. That may well be so, but it would be extremely helpful if the representatives of the Canadian people could consider the information on the United States internal food-aid program and the views of our Department of Agriculture in respect thereto. Perhaps then we could come to a conclusion as to the cost and, what is far more important to us as representatives of Canadians, the benefits to Canadian citizens.
If the hon. member was speaking in terms of overproduction, let me point out that we who represent western constituencies face the problem of overproduction in terms of wheat. Like the farmers in Quebec who have overproduction in a certain area which I will not go into, nothing would make us happier than to have a program carried out by the Department of Agriculture to increase the number of consumers. If the figures the hon. member mentioned are correct, this would pour some $250 million into the agricultural sector of the economy and give our farmers a reasonable return on their production, as well as increased internal consumption.
U.S. Internal Food-Aid Program
As representatives of the agricultural sector of our economy, we are fundamentally interested in any kind of food program which would enhance the internal markets of Canada such as the program undertaken in the United States. If we could put $250 million into our agricultural sector, I would be most happy and excited about such a program. It would get the economy rolling in terms of putting money into the hands of western and eastern producers, to be followed by a flow of money into the hands of the industrial sector as a result of increased purchasing power.
In order to make decisions, we as Members of Parliament must be able to examine studies undertaken and documents relating to them. Many studies which have been made of the agricultural sector in relation to food and food consumption have been hidden in the offices of ministers; Members of Parliament have not been allowed to look at them. One such study was made for the small farms development consolidation program, papers in respect of which I have asked for in a motion for the production of papers that has been on the order paper for months. These papers have not been produced-yet members are asked to deal with legislation such as Bill C-5 in connection with agriculture.
Documents are sent to provincial governments and are looked at by federal civil servants. Members of Parliament and the Canadian people, however, are not allowed to examine such documents. If we wish to take another example in terms of the agricultural sector, the Department of Agriculture and the Wheat Board, we need only consider the whole question of national transportation and the policy drawn up, with the involvement of the Canada Grains Council, the Canadian Wheat Board, the railroads and the line elevator companies, which has been turned over to the provincial governments and which the minister in charge of the Wheat Board said last spring would be tabled in the House of Commons very soon. That transportation study has not yet been tabled in the House of Commons for consideration by Members of Parliament.
I can see great possibilities, in terms of business, in a Canadian internal food-aid program. Western producers, above all other groups, I suppose, in terms of grain, have faced great difficulties in certain years because of their dependence on the international market. A vast percentage of the grain and wheat sold from western Canada and, I suppose, a great percentage of eastern soft wheat, is sold on the international market. If an internal food-aid program would enhance the domestic market for farm produce, this would be a way in which western and eastern producers could see an improvement of their financial position and encouragement in their desire to remain on the land.
The hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway did an excellent job in pointing out some of the difficulties in terms of proper nutrition and proper diet for child raising, and so on. I shall not go into that matter. I hope that when I resume my seat the question of producing this report for those of us who represent farmers, and for the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway and my friend across the way, members who have an interest in nutri-

July 6, 1972
U.S. Internal Food-Aid Program
tion as well as the income of producers, will be considered favourably.
I hope, also, that when I resume my seat, Mr. Speaker, you will either allow the question to come to a vote or there will be unanimous consent of the House that this document be produced. I rest my case on the good graces of government members.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first I wish to thank the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mrs. Maclnnis) for introducing this motion. I have listened very carefully to her comments and more often than once, I was reminded of the days when I was a student in agricultural sciences at the University of Montreal attending nutrition courses.
I commend the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway for having drawn the House's attention to this ever important situation. I also wish to congratulate her for her work in various committees. I have seen her at work in the Health, Welfare and Social Affairs Committee where social problems were considered as well as problems related to packing and consumers' protection. It is my wish that after the forthcoming great event, the Liberal party will include several female members.
Having said this, I cannot however agree with the comments made by the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway in connection with the tabling of the documents mentioned in her notice of motion. I would invite the hon. member to read the reply given to her by the Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Jerome) as recorded on page 1280 of our proceedings of November 18, 1970, and I quote:
Mr. Speaker, on behalf of the Minister of Agriculture I may advise the hon. member that no formal report has ever been made by the Department of Agriculture on the United States internal food aid program and its application to Canada.
I suggest that this was not a report, but rather a draft study, and, as pointed out by the Parliamentary Secretary, various departments when it comes to drafting important legislation, usually consider pilot projects so as to determine the feasibility of any specific program.
I think hunger always raises problems, and no human being can remain insensitive to it. Therefore, I would not like the hon. member to think that members of this House are insensitive to the situation which she brought to our attention.
Now, as far as the report is concerned, there are several studies in the United States which deal precisely with the experiment with food distribution, and those studies are available to the public, providing the hon. member can ask for them.

At the present time the United States operates four major food-aid programs. The first is the commodity distribution program, the second is the national school lunch program, the third is the special milk program and the fourth is the food stamp program. All four programs are administered by Consumer Food Programs of the USDA Consumer and Marketing Service. The special milk pro-

gram and the food stamp program are examples of food assistance programs which operate on a cash grant for local food purchases. Under the special milk program, federal cash grants are utilized to reduce the cost of milk to children in elementary and secondary schools.
The food stamp program, on the other hand, enables needy families to purchase food stamps which have a redeemable value greater than the purchase price. The difference between the purchase price and the redeemable value represents the federal cash contribution. Both of these programs are based on the assumption that if the food purchasing power of the recipient is increased, food consumption will also increase provided that provisions have been made to guard against substitution for regular food purchases.

To come back, Mr. Speaker, to the problems raised by the hon. member, I do not think we should compare this program with the situation which prevails in the United States and Canada, precisely because of differences in the social policies of those two countries. In Canada, we have a highly developed social policy, including a family allowances policy established for the benefit of school-aged children. If some provinces want to experiment with milk distribution in schools-and I think this problem has been raised on many occasions in Quebec-this comes under their own jurisdiction. If they want to distribute milk in schools, they are entirely free to do so.
The main issue raised by the hon. member for Fron-tenac (Mr. Corriveau) is that of budget administration. If a family lives on a weekly budget of $75 or $100, its wellbeing will indeed depend on the nutrition value of the products the housewife can buy. As underlined also by the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway, more information should be provided at the level of the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs and at the level of the various associations and citizens' committees. The caisses populaires are now doing excellent information work on the nutrition value of the farm products.
Considering their energy and protein value, farm products are available to the consumer at quite reasonable prices. According to an opinion often voiced by the producers, Canada is a "cheap country for food". If we consider prices paid in recent years, broilers sold at 18 cents a pound, eggs at 30 cents a dozen and pork at 24 cents a pound. These are certainly not exorbitant prices.
Our aim should indeed be to try to disseminate more information on nutrition through foodstuffs and especially on comparative prices for various beef cuts. While a student and working in a butcher's shop, I could see to what extent the housewife was poorly informed on meat; she bought some cuts priced at $1.50, whereas, considering equivalent nutrition value, she could have purchased others costing three times less. The question is rather that of educating the consumers on the nutrition value of foods, on the various meat cuts and on the price. I believe we should center our efforts in that area.
I shall refer the hon. member to several departmental publications which are designed to further inform consumers about the purchasing and unit price of various
July 6, 1972

consumer products. Some booklets are available at the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs, and there are a few excellent ones as well in the Department of Agriculture. Various agricultural television programs were produced with a view to assist the housewife, so that she may get at a fair price several agricultural products, such as poultry, milk, eggs, fruit or vegetable. If such was the case, we should only have reached part of the hon. member's objective.
I think, Mr. Speaker, that we should consider very carefully the whole thing, because, as I stated earlier, we, as human beings, cannot overlook the problem of hunger in the world.
The hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Knight) spoke about the grain production. I shall only refer to the assistance given by Canada to under developed countries. As far as international food-aid program is concerned, the contribution of Canada amounts to about $95 million. I suggest that we should increase this amount, but once more, we should do it according to our ability to pay.
This was an outline of the situation, and as I stated at the outset of my remarks, I cannot agree with the remarks made by the hon. member about the motion now before us, which reads as follows:
That an Order of the House do issue for a copy of the report undertaken in the Department of Agriculture on the United States Internal Food-Aid Program and its application to Canada.
It was rather a survey. I do not object that these compilations be used as a work paper by the ministry and its officials in order to eventually implement, if such implementation is deemed really important, a program similar to that which has been tried in the United States. To me, this was more of a survey than of a report.
Here again, Canada has played its part in the field of assistance provided to needy families. But I think that the situation is quite different from that which prevails in the United States. We have a social policy, a family allowance program directed to children, but I think that we should put great emphasis on information and popularization so that housewives would know not only the unit price of the food products they buy, but also their nutrition value and protein content.

Mr. Chairman, when we ended our discussion at five o'clock I had been trying to point out to the minister and to members of the committee the difficulties which in my opinion face the longshoremen in the powers which apparently the minister insists on giving to the arbitrator with regard to the job security plans now in the collective agreement.
I do not want to speak any longer because no purpose can be served by repeating the arguments. I merely say to the minister that management and the union agreed to the job security plans last April, before this year's shipping season started, and the longshoremen have the right that those provisions be retained in full next year. There is no reason why the abritrator should have the power to change those provisions so as to weaken the job security plans for the years 1973 and 1974. I have said all I could say. I had hoped the minister would agree to bring in a proposal to deal with this question, but since he has not I move the following amendment:
That clause 7 be amended by changing the period at the end of line 28 to a comma and by adding immediately thereafter the following words:
"provided that he does not make any modifications in the plans
set out in the collective agreements as such plans apply to the
years 1973 and 1974."

I do not want to repeat the arguments which were made this afternoon when it was pointed out that the agreement worked out between the union and the employers provided a formula for job security for the years 1972, 1973 and 1974. Difficulties have arisen in implementing the plan for this year because several important months, in terms of work on the docks and therefore of payments into the fund from which the work guarantee would be provided, have gone by.
I cannot see why there should be any proposal by the employers or by the government that any person, be it the government, an employer or an arbitrator, should do anything to vary the agreement which has already been worked out and which was agreed to by both employers and employees in reference to the years 1973 and 1974.

Mr. Chairman, in recent months the people of Canada have heard a great deal about the supposed exorbitant, unreasonable demands made by various labour groups. I point out to the minister and to members of the committee that the guarantee which the longshoremen will get for employment and earnings is something like $167 a week for 37 weeks a year. My arithmetic shows that to be just over $6,000 a year. Montreal is the largest city in Canada and its cost of living is amongst the highest of any city in Canada. I suggest to the minister and members of this committee that a longshoreman or any other worker who has to live in the city of Montreal on just over $6,000 a year in 1973 or 1974 will not have a very affluent life.
Mr. Chairman, I simply cannot understand why the minister should now be proposing that an arbitrator might be able to reopen the agreement which has been reached, and to scale down what I consider to be a very modest income guarantee for any worker in the year 1973.

Mr. Chairman, we went over this ground quite extensively this afternoon. The hon. member for Winnipeg North was not present to hear the exchange, but he will find the explanations in Hansard that I gave then to support the provision set out in clause 7. I have given a good deal of thought to this matter and have looked carefully at the proposition the hon. member for York South has brought forward. We have considered it most carefully. We have considered the equities involved and after a brief excursion down that road, which has its attractions, we have returned to favour the present proposition as being one that provides the greatest justice. We must remember that we must provide justice for both parties; there must be equity for both parties. That will be in the best interests of all in future.
The hon. member for York South has brought forward an amendment. However, I must confess to some puzzlement because in speaking to it he opened up another door, and when you go through that door I think you will find that you are going beyond the whole purpose of this bill, certainly beyond the provisions with respect to the arbitrator's authority as provided in the bill. He would be putting the working people, for whom he has expressed concern, into greater jeopardy in the years 1973 and 1974 than any that might be contemplated in this bill.
If I understood the hon. member correctly, at the close of the debate this afternoon he was saying that we ought to make a provision in the bill so that the minister, on petition of one of the parties to the collective agreement, would automatically be able to appoint an arbitrator to modify the agreements in 1973 and 1974. We are not giving any such right for modification of that kind in those future years.
As I understand it, there would be the automatic appointment of an arbitrator of those collective agreements if certain events arose. What are those certain events? As was suggested this afternoon, it might be the plea of the employers that for one reason or another they could not live up to the income security plan, the plan that pays for 37 weeks whether they work or not under the new regime; they could not pay for it and they would be financially embarrassed. Am I to then appoint another arbitrator to open up the whole matter again? Are we to be in continual insecurity in this one field of arbitration? Even if we agreed that was a good proceeding-and I immediately say it is not-would we not be going beyond
July 6, 1972

the whole purpose of this bill, which is not to cure hypothetical events which might occur in the future? What the bill is intended to do, and I read from its title, is as follows:
An act to provide for the resumption of the operation of the ports-
Our whole objective is to provide for the resumption of the operation of the ports. Surely we would be going beyond what we agreed to on second reading, the principle of this bill, in providing in addition that in some future eventuality which we are unable to foresee at this time we should open up and modify the collective agreement.

subtopic: ST. LAWRENCE PORTS OPERATIONS BILL MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR RESUMPTION OF LONGSHORING AND RELATED OPERATIONS
