The hon. member says that is not what his amendment does. I am glad he has retreated to the confines of his amendment. When he spoke, he went beyond that. We ought to have that perfectly clear in our minds if we are seeking the best interests of the men as well as of the employers, as we must. If it is to be a viable agreement in the future we should not introduce into anything we do any jeopardy down through the succeeding years.
I earnestly hope that the decision can be made soon. I do not mean five months from now, or next year; I mean very soon-as soon as the arbitrator is in a position to judge the operations and, therefore, the facts of the case to make the job security plan viable. All that we are providing at this point in time is that at the earliest possible moment the arbitrator will make his decision. That is his "once only" decision with regard to income security; he will not have another opportunity. He will look as far into the future as he is able to do objectively and he will make his judgment.
I earnestly hope, and I think it is the hope of all members, that when the arbitrator fixes the date for the start of the job security provisions it will be the earliest date feasible, and when he fixes the terminal date beyond which the modifications will not apply that will be the earliest feasible date to make this a viable plan as required in clause 7. It is quite conceivable that it will be in 1972; but I am entering on delicate ground and I know that none of us would wish that. That is for him to decide. However, in the nature of the circumstances I think it is quite reasonable to expect that he will know what we consider to be an early decision, an early date to begin and an early date to terminate the modifications.
If we in Parliament set a date either to begin or to terminate, we take a judgment upon ourselves that we know something about the facts, something about the matter of dispute and we are capable of saying "the end of this year and no longer." It may be longer. I earnestly hope it will be shorter; I expect it will be. However, that is territory upon which it would be imprudent for us as Members of Parliament to trespass at this time in considering this bill.

I note that the hon. member who sits behind me thinks that so long as someone from his party has spoken, anybody else should shut up. That is their attitude. They have had their say and everybody else should be quiet. However, I will say that I deplore the fact that this Parliament has had to engage in another example of scrambling "ad hockery", because that is what this bill is.
When we were considering Bill C-183 I made several speeches to emphasize what I consider to be one of the greatest gaps in the Canada Labour Code, and I reemphasize to the government that the biggest gap is that there is no provision to take care of the public interest. As the hon. member for York South (Mr. Lewis) said, the public interest in this case overrode the interest of management and of collective bargaining.

The individuals over there who sit like crows on a fence and shout "Sit down" should make a contribution other than sitting in their place. But they do not. All they do is delay this matter further, because we will have our say.
As I said, the biggest difficulty that faces the country insofar as labour relations are concerned is that there is nothing here that permits the government to act when the greater public interest is being pushed aside or suppressed. We had the example of Parliament sitting right up to the eve of Christmas because of the strike of airline mechanics. The same sort of thing occurred when electronics workers in the public service were holding to ransom the greater public interest.
July 6, 1972

Some people ask, "Are you going to impose compulsory arbitration?" What is this but compulsory arbitration? This is forcing people back to work. Parliament, after it is pushed and prodded, takes action far too late. Millions of dollars are lost to the dockers and to their employers and the economic future of the port of Montreal is placed in great jeopardy.
I was amazed at the temperance of my colleague, the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Alexander), in his criticism of the government. He was very moderate in his criticism of the minister. He should have climbed over there with spurs to deal with the government which, quite frankly, has been very lax and very slow in dealing with this matter. I support my colleague, the hon. member for Sainte-Marie (Mr. Valade), who suggested that what should apply in a strike of this kind is a mandatory secret ballot. I understand that the secret ballot was used in two of the ports, certainly in the port of Quebec, and there was less trouble there. There is certainly far less trouble when there is a secret ballot, and in matters of this kind it is mandatory that it be a supervised ballot: the public interest demands that.
This bill does not impose any penalties for non-compliance. Someone asked why these should be necessary because penalties are already provided in the Criminal Code. We saw in this morning's press that some penalties have been imposed with regard to this dispute. But how were they applied? They were applied under a very contentious provision in the law, namely, contempt of court. I know that organized labour does not like the provision of contempt of court, but we are relying on that and I think it is a very shaky base. The Criminal Code also deals with the individual. It seems to me that in this legislation, or in the labour code, penalties should be defined far more clearly in respect of union organizations or employers of organized labour so that if in the public interest action must be taken, it is spelled out and everybody knows what it is.
It seems to me that this debate has been an exercise of two days which should not have taken place. I am not assessing blame to one side or the other: I suppose that both sides are to blame. But I do complain because Parliament has had to engage in what I call a scramble of "ad hockery". This may happen more frequently during this year. That is not the way to deal with this type of labour dispute. I am hopeful that everybody will have some sense now and that they will repair as quickly as possible the grave economic damage that has occurred to a section of the country.

Mr. Speaker, this is a piece of legislation about which no one can be happy. We have observed that the minister himself has become increasingly unhappy with it. As a matter of fact, listening to him on certain broadcasts he seemed really desperate in his stridency, trying to apologize for the legislation. Social workers across the country are not happy about this legislation. The opposition parties, for various reasons, are not happy about it. The one million mothers from whom family allowances will be withdrawn are not happy about it. Taxpayers who have really studied the matter are not happy about it. With all these people unhappy and worried about this family allowance bill, one is driven to inquire why the government introduced a bill of this type.
The government took a long time to get around to it. The government examined the matter and introduced variations of this bill. Finally it reached the tail end of this session and, with great reluctance, the government introduced the bill knowing that nearly all the people concerned feel miserable about it. If all this is the case, why has the government sought to push through this legislation at this stage? It is for the sole and simple reason that the government is unwilling to deal with the question of poverty in the way in which it should be dealt with; it is

July 6, 1972
Family Income Security Plan
unwilling to take the type of measures which should be taken if poverty is to be eliminated.
The government is unwilling to face up to the need for a proper quaranteed income plan, a plan whereby people are quaranteed jobs and can make a living according to their abilities. Above all, the government is unwilling to introduce a fair system of taxation by which it could pay for such measures.
This is a crummy piece of legislation, a crummy way of dealing with family allowances. It is unworthy and inadequate no matter what way you look at it. In fact, what the legislation is doing is taking advantage of the desperation of poor people in order to appeal to the sympathy of other elements to get this thing passed. It is an inadequate thing; it is unfair; it is unjust; it is a poor piece of planning. Yet the government is leaning on other sections of the population by appealing to the desperation of the poor people who need more money.
There is no doubt that poor people need more money, and the government is telling the poor people that this is the only way they can get more money at this time. The government has gone to the anti-poverty organizations, to people on low incomes, and said, "This is your only chance for more income." Naturally, people who are on social assistance, people in low income brackets, are frightened silly. In turn they say, "If this is the only way the government will give us any more revenue, then we have to pass this bill." They have sent desperate wires to all members of this House urging us not to stand in the way of their getting more money at this time. I think that is completely unworthy of the government.
The government is counting on people outside this House not knowing the facts. It is telling them that this is the only way to get started on a guaranteed income scheme. Mr. Speaker, this is as far from a guaranteed income scheme as is the city of Ottawa from Timbuctoo. It has nothing to do with a guaranteed income scheme. The principle of a guaranteed income scheme is the establishment of a definite income floor below which nobody will be allowed to fall. This bill is a handout, a pittance to the poor: it has no resemblance at all to a guaranteed income scheme. This is no way to get started on a guaranteed income scheme. In fact, this is a way of avoiding putting a guaranteed income scheme into operation. It is an obstacle in the way of facing up to a guaranteed income scheme.
If you look at the areas which are desperate to get this legislation passed, they are the areas where there are people who desperately need money. The government has turned a deaf ear and a blind eye to them in their poverty, and they see this bill as their one remaining chance. What the government is not telling the poor is probably more important still. It is not telling poor people that under this proposed scheme the new levels of payments cannot be made for at least a year. When the minister introduced this scheme he was confident that the new rates would come into force this summer. But as his officials began to experiment with the procedures necessary to make the legislation effective, they found that the appalling processes of red tape and the complications of administration were putting the legislation farther and farther away from coming into operation. Today the departmental offi-

cials tell us that it will be at least a year before the bill can come into operation. That is something which the government is not telling poor people. It is not telling them that their desperation for more money must continue for at least another year.
Further, it is not telling them that the new schedule of payments will not even have the buying power of a 1945 family allowance cheque. Between July, 1945, and September, 1971, the consumer price index rose to 230.7. This means that the family allowance for a child 11 years of age should have risen from $7 per month in July, 1945, to $16.15 in September, 1971. Instead, under this bill a child of 11 will get only $15, and only if it is a single child and the family income is less than $4,500.
A family with a working wife will be penalized. If a husband is making $4,000 a year and his wife supplements his income by a mere $1,000, and they have only one child, then the baby bonus will decrease. This new scheme is not only a pittance to the poor; it is a guarantee that they will lose all incentive to work their way out of the trap of poverty. That is what this baby bonus amounts to.
This government is not telling the poor that in this legislation there is no protection against the provinces cutting off their social assistance by the amount that this family allowance would raise it. There is no protection in this legislation to ensure that poor families will get the full amount. The provinces are perfectly free under this legislation to cut down the allowance for social assistance by the amount that this family allowance would have increased it. Let me point out what this means in.practice. Recently I received a letter from some poor people in the city of Calgary, the Anti-Poverty Organization, who wrote:
The bill provides for a redistribution of family allowance payments. Poorer families will receive an increase in family allowance. Because of the increase in moneys involved, there is a proposal that family allowance now be treated as an income, and income tax be paid. In certain areas we feel this to be fair and just. But in other areas, it is not. Particularly when a family is forced, by circumstance, to subsist on social assistance.
Traditionally, the family allowance payments have never been viewed as income. Therefore, they have been exempt from being so considered by welfare agencies and have not been deducted from assistance cheques. Should they be now viewed as an income they will be deducted. In simple mathematics this might mean that a woman with six children today receives a total of $40 from family allowance per month. Her monthly social assistance maximum cheque might possibly be $275. This gives her an actual cash flow of $310. This is true under present administrative policies. Yet, with an increase payment scaled to her over-all income, this mother may now (under Bill C-264) receive about $160 monthly from family allowance. Viewed as an income it then would be deducted from the $275 social assistance cheque; she would now get $160 in family allowance and $125 in social assistance for a total of $275.
In other words, in Edmonton or Calgary she now gets a total of $310 but when this bill goes through there is nothing in the world to stop officials cutting her, with her six children, down to $275.1 raised this point in committee on May 24, 1972, when the matter came up and I should like to quote from the proceedings so that people will see what the government is not telling them. At page 9:21 I said:
I want to know whether any attempt has been made to ensure that
July 6, 1972

in any discussions with the provinces that when the people get this family allowance legislation, that people in social assistance families getting this amount will not be taken off the rates that are set for social assistance. Have there been discussions with the provinces on this? I know in my own province there would be very great danger that in getting the social assistance rates this particular form of income would be taken into account and deducted from what otherwise would be given.
The minister replied:
There have been discussions to the degree that I have expressed to the provinces when we have talked about this principle of selectivity and getting larger benefits to those in the lower income groups the hope that it would not be deducted dollar for dollar from social assistance levels that are now being paid to families in Canada. It seemed to me that I received protestations from many social welfare ministers that this would not be the case. They would not do this.
I pressed the minister still further and he replied:
That is the only way you can do it. You can hope that that will not be the case. Provinces, as you know, have jurisdiction in this field in terms of the administration of social assistance, and we cannot tell them what to do. We can only hope that they will not do it. So I can only express my own view, I do not think they will do it.
I then pointed out that when dealing with the province of Quebec the minister went throught the whole painful negotiation to ensure that certain points would be observed in the legislation in order to suit that province. I said I could not see, if he could go through the process of negotiation with the province of Quebec in order to get certain guarantees, why he could not go through the process of negotiation with other provinces. He should make sure that the full amount that was being given under the new family allowance would go straight to those people on social assistance for whom it was intended, and that it would not be cut off by the provincial authorities in setting the social assistance rates. The minister insisted that this could not be done and that he was hoping the authorities would not do it in the provinces.
Yesterday in a statement the minister pointed out that in the case of the old age pension the regulations under the Canada Assistance Plan had been altered so that the provincial authorities could deduct those rates. I am pointing out that it is only a matter of time until the provincial authorities also cut down the family allowance to the point where the people might as well not get it. The government is not telling the poor people that they are completely unprotected, as far as Ottawa is concerned, in the new family allowance rate. In my view this is not honest and it is not playing fair with the people for whom this legislation was designed.
Another thing they are not telling the poor people is that this legislation means perpetual paperwork on their part. Every time a child moves from below age 12 to above age 12 a report has to be made. Every time a child moves beyond age 17 a report has to be made to the authorities. Every time a child is born there is a report to the authorities. Every time a child dies there is a report to the authorities. Every time there is a change in the family income there is a report to the authorities. Every time a wife goes out to work for income there is a report to the authorities. Every time a husband goes on unemployment insurance there is a report to the authorities. What is being added to the arthritis of government procedures?
Family Income Security Plan
We are getting a Saint Vitus's dance of administrative complexities added, making this into a complete mess.

subtopic: MEASURES TO PROVIDE BENEFITS IN RESPECT OF CHILDREN
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: MEASURES TO PROVIDE BENEFITS IN RESPECT OF CHILDREN
speechtext:
1 think this is the height of dishonesty when it comes to dealing with people, particularly the most vulnerable element of the population. Above all, what the government is not telling the people is that in order to get this pittance for the poor it was completely unnecessary to replace a good, universal plan. We in this party have an amendment and we have been prepared to compromise by placing one amendment now before the House. We have said, "All right; you are insisting that you cannot do this in the right way, so keep the universal family allowance for everybody and then add for the poor people the new amounts. If you are serious about the poor people needing this, and if you will not do anything else, then our amendment says keep the universal scheme and add on the amounts for the poor people who qualify." But the government will not accept that amendment either. We appeal to them to accept it if they will not accept anything else.
I want to make a last appeal to the minister. It is a very serious thing to wreck this universal scheme that we have had. There are only two things wrong with it. First of all, the amounts are away out of line with what they should be. There is another thing that the government is not telling the people, Mr. Speaker. There is no escalation clause in the family allowance scheme such as has appeared in legislation for veterans and old people.
The inflationary factors that are working against all the people will work against those being paid benefits under this plan. What is wrong with the legislation is that the amounts provided are far too small and there are no provisions for escalating them as living costs rise. Also, no attempt is made to distribute the burden fairly. Taxation will not fall most heavily on those who can best bear it. Actually, a great many families that are being taxed to provide moneys for family allowances will never get any. The million mothers who are to be denied benefits will pay for this measure in taxes. As I say, they will not get any benefits at all.
This plan is a far, far cry from the plan of 1944. The Liberal government of the day then introduced the universal family allowance scheme. They were proud they had introduced it and held their heads high, even though they had been prodded from behind by the party I support. They were proud because the principles underlying that legislation were good. The government recognized that families with children had special needs. That was no attempt at dealing with poverty in any sort of bad way because the payments were directed to all the mothers of this country. We recognized that they were doing a service for Canada and we were prepared to help them perform that service.
I have met university graduates in the last little while who have told me that it was family allowances saved over the years which helped to pay for their education. That, of course, was part of the original intent. We also intended to ensure a greater measure of equality for all

July 6, 1972
Family Income Security Plan
children in this country. We intended to help ensure an adequate income for social insurance and social assistance recipients with children while at the same time avoiding grants that would diminish incentives to work. Further, we intended to create a substantial program for maintaining high levels of income and employment in the post-war period. This program worked well for years.
As I suggested, if the minister had been content to increase payments and bring them into line with today's living costs, if he had included an escalation clause to take care of future developments and had introduced a fair taxation scheme to be implemented either by way of general taxation or special, selective taxation as the Canadian Council on Social Development proposed, we would not harbour sad or unhappy thoughts about this legislation. That, however, has not been done.
Furthermore, we now see this universal scheme going the way of the former old age pension universal scheme. Again I say, the million mothers who will not get benefits will feel keenly the injustice of their position. Remember, the Royal Commission on the Status of Women recommended increased family allowances, as has committee after committee and commission after commission in this country. They said we should not withdraw family allowances from some but, rather, should increase them for all.
Carrying out the program will be an administrative nightmare. Altogether, this will be a ghastly failure. As the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) predicted some time ago, I too predict that it will not be many years before this government-or, what is more likely, the government that will succeed it-will look with shame at this type of allowance as being completely unworthy of the families, households and firesides of this country. Then they will say, "What in the world were they thinking of in 1972?"
We are living in a rich country. We are boasting every year of our increasing gross national product, of our increase in productivity. We boast of our standing among the nations of the world. Practically all nations which call themselves civilized have adopted universal family allowance schemes. But Canada is going back and joining the underdeveloped countries in this regard. I am ashamed of that and I feel sure that in his heart the minister shares that feeling of shame. He, too, is disappointed.
With these words, I again appeal to the minister to look again at this program. It is not too late to change. Often at the last minute people have drawn back and changed their minds. History has shown that they had the courage to do what their conscience dictated. They came through the immediate ordeal and were looked on as men of courage and vision.

subtopic: MEASURES TO PROVIDE BENEFITS IN RESPECT OF CHILDREN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, whether or not the revival of Bill C-170 will bring about the desired results will depend on the attitude of all Members of Parliament towards its objectives, which are to provide for the payment of benefits in respect of children. I see no purpose in repeating again the many weaknesses and inequities in the bill. My main purpose in speaking on the amendment of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) is to remind all hon. members that, while we procrastinate in

continuous debate on the bill, hundreds of thousands of Canadian children are being denied the increased benefits provided for under the bill.

subtopic: MEASURES TO PROVIDE BENEFITS IN RESPECT OF CHILDREN
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: MEASURES TO PROVIDE BENEFITS IN RESPECT OF CHILDREN
speechtext:
The Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Munro), who I realize feels very strongly that the bill is acceptable in its present form, has shown a stubborn attitude in not accepting some amendments which my party introduced during the report stage and which would have improved the bill. It is obvious now that he will not relent and accede to these requests. For example, Mr. Speaker, I see no reason why the official opposition's amendment to have cheques made out to mothers was not acceptable, since we would only be repeating what was contained in the old Family Allowances Act. Neither can I see the reasoning behind the government's refusal to accept an amendment which would only fulfil a commitment made by the government under Bill C-264, namely, that increases in benefits would be payable as of May 1,
1972.	Although I have repeated this many times, I will continue to repeat it: the government made a promise to the families involved and they failed to keep that promise. The promise was that whenever this bill became law the government would owe Canadians who qualified some $13 million a month since May 1, 1972.
Another serious fault is that the minister has failed to ensure that provinces will not include income under FISP and set that off against social assistance. Unless remedial action is taken before FISP is enacted, the provisions of the Canada Assistance Plan could undermine completely the stated objectives of FISP, which are to fight poverty. The problem, in a nutshell, is that under the Canada Assistance Plan the provinces are perfectly entitled to lower their rates of welfare assistance to families in proportion to the higher family allowance payments that these families will be receiving when FISP becomes law.
Under section 2(b)(iii) of the Canada Assistance Plan there is provision that the provinces, in determining the degree of need and in making arrangements for social assistance to applicants for welfare, shall take into account all income maintenance payments made through unemployment insurance, old age pension security payments, the Canada Pension Plan and guaranteed income supplement schemes. However, it is optional for the provinces to take into account family allowances and other schemes. This is a decision for each individual province to make.
Certainly, not one of the provinces calculates family allowance payments as income for purposes of social assistance. However, it is entirely possible that when the new, higher benefits to poorer families are paid after FISP becomes law, some provinces may start to include FISP as part of the welfare applicant's income and will lower family social assistance payments correspondingly. It is especially likely that the poorer provinces which have long felt hard pressed by the inflexible 50-50 cost-sharing arrangement entered into with the federal government under the Canada Assistance Plan will unfortunately feel compelled to make such a revision.
July 6, 1972

Family allowances seem to be making some headway in dealing with regional and individual poverty, but this problem threatens to erode the gains made unless agreement is reached between the two governments. I hope that in the time available to the minister he will ensure that arrangements are made and agreements are reached with the provinces.
Another matter that has not been mentioned so far is the appeal procedure. This should be revamped. The plans for appeal under a new FISP, clause 11 of Bill C-264, are for a government-appointed, government-run tribunal to hear complaints about receipt and amounts of benefits. To ensure that the appeal procedure is conducted in a fair and just manner the tribunal established to hear appeals should instead be quite independent of the government and should not be merely another subsection of the government.
Many members who spoke in the various phases of the debate have pointed out other weaknesses in the bill, but at no time has there been a satisfactory explanation as to how the government will deal with drastic changes in income each year for citizens such as fishermen, farmers and independent truckers. The income floor will be based on the previous year's income. Let me give an example of a fisherman who qualifies for the maximum benefits during a bad fishing year. In the second year he might have a reasonable income. This might put him over the basic income floor. After the fishing season he may find that, based on his income, he will not qualify for that year. In the third season he might have another bad year with little or no income. He may have to resort to unemployment insurance or even welfare. This means that fisherman would have to repay the government for the previous year's benefits when it would be impossible for him to do so, even with the fancy computers available to figure this out for the government. What will this fisherman do?
My concern is that while this bill has dragged on, we have failed to realize the intent, that is, to provide increases in benefits to those with children who are on the no-income or low-income scale. No one seems to be particularly concerned that while we procrastinate, at this very moment hundreds of thousands of children are suffering from malnutrition because of lack of proper food. At this very moment thousands of Canadian children do not have a decent bed on which to sleep. They huddle for warmth in corners of substandard homes, cold and miserable, because the government has failed to provide decent housing for Canadians.
No one seems to want to realize that at this very moment thousands of parents in this country are sacrificing their health from undernourishment in order to give a little extra to their children because governments have failed to provide for them. These parents sit and wonder why we, who are supposed to provide them with care when they are unable to do so, have failed over the years to deal effectively with poverty when, as everyone admits, this should be the most prosperous country in the world.
May I call it ten o'clock, Mr. Speaker?

TRANSPORT-LEASING OF UNITED STATES BOXCARS TO MOVE GRAIN-PURCHASE OF ADDITIONAL HOPPER CARS BY RAILWAYS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on April 21 I asked the Minister of Transport (Mr. Jamieson) a question relating to the leasing of United States boxcars for the handling of grain. The minister informed me that the CNR was leasing boxcars. I asked a supplementary question concerning the fact that the CNR was spending millions of dollars on building flat cars in Montreal while we needed hopper cars for the movement of western grain. The minister said he would look into the matter and deal with the subject when talking with officials of the CNR at a future date.
The situation in terms of hopper cars has changed somewhat since that time, in the sense that the government has decided to build about 2,000 hopper cars to meet the needs of moving western grain and leasing them through the Canadian Wheat Board. I and other members have asked the government on a number of occasions to impress upon the railroads the need of putting hopper cars into service for the movement of grain. I am pleased to see that this has been done. There is some question about whether or not the Wheat Board, in providing the cars for the government, is in some way subsidizing the railways. I do not wish to get into that question tonight.
Since this may well be the second last day before adjourning for the summer, I want to point out that there are still a number of key problems with regard to the grain movement in the west. I propose to present some of these problems in the hope that the government will look at them even though the House may tomorrow adjourn for the summer. On several occasions I have brought a real problem to the attention of the Minister of Transport and the minister in charge of the Wheat Board. It is that at CNR delivery points in the province of Saskatchewan, particularly at nine delivery points in southern Saskatchewan, there has been a real shortage of grain doors. One quite accomplished writer for the Globe and Mail asked what is a grain door. You can have all the boxcars you want at a delivery point, but if you do not have a grain door to put in the boxcar you can not move the grain from the delivery point.
The CNR, which has a public responsibility because it is a public corporation, at one time this spring had 40,000 grain doors in a warehouse in Saskatoon. They were unaware of the fact they were supposed to be repairing
3856

July 6, 1972
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion
them to be used at delivery points in Saskatchewan. That kind of lack of priority by the CNR has to be taken care of for the benefit of farmers trying to meet their quotas, as well as for the benefit of the grain buyer at the local delivery point so that he is not sitting up all night preparing grain doors instead of loading the boxcars. Some hon. members who are not from the west may not find that 'moortant but it is pretty basic to moving grain that you have proper grain doors at the shipping points.
The other problem at the shipping points is the condition of the boxcars which the railways send back after having been to the terminals at Vancouver. It takes many hours to repair them. That is coupled with the problem of terminating quotas. Members from the west are aware that there is some need for terminating quotas in order to meet our commitment and the present demands of our foreign markets. The terminating quota has created some difficulty because at particular delivery points farmers cannot get their grains into the elevator because of problems such as boxcar allocation. Because of the terminating dates they lose their quota in moving, for example, 2CW Durum wheat. They can lose their quota because the boxcars have not been allocated.
As this may be the second last day of this Parliament, I hope the ministers involved will give serious consideration to the extension of quotas, particularly in situations where the farmers are unable to meet their quotas because of boxcar allocations. Further, representatives of the Wheat Board stated before the newly-formed Senate committee on agriculture, of which the former member for Assiniboia is chairman, that they would take the question of the extension of the quotas into consideration. I hope they will do so, having given this undertaking.
There are other aspects which must concern us in relation to the movement of western grain. For example, there are the experiments which have been going on at the inland terminals. I trust that the information forthcoming from these activities will be made available not only to western producers who, incidentally, may well be paying for these experiments indirectly through the Wheat Board, but to all Members of Parliament and to the public at large.

maintopic: REGIONAL ECONOMIC EXPANSION-REQUEST THAT SHERBROOKE BE DESIGNATED AS SPECIAL AREA
REGIONAL ECONOMIC EXPANSION-REQUEST THAT SHERBROOKE BE DESIGNATED AS SPECIAL AREA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on June 22, I asked a question to the hon. Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Marchand) in connection with the Sherbrooke area. I asked him whether Sherbrooke was going to be designated as a "special area", in view of the large number of very poor adjacent parishes located in this region.
My constituency is partly included in the Sherbrooke area; in view of the current economic situation, I urge the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion to give the Sherbrooke region the status of "special area".
Since several destitute parishes in my region are within the Sherbrooke area from the point of view of the economy, I wonder whether it would not be possible to designate the city of Sherbrooke as a "special area". If not, I would like to make another suggestion to the hon. minister or to his parliamentary secretary.
Would it be possible for parishes in my riding to be detached from the Sherbrooke area? I think of the Scots-town parish which is quite destitute. There are many destitute parishes, but I take this one as an example. Formerly, a rather important industry was operating there employing 400 people. This industry has shut down and no other has been established in this municipality which is now deserted and deprived of everything. A visit there is nothing funny. It is part of the Sherbrooke area and nothing can be done for it.
I would like, if possible, that Sherbrooke become a "special area" encompassing all these municipalities, or alternatively that all parishes in the Compton riding be detached from Sherbrooke to become a "special area" since what happened to Scotstown is being repeated in many parishes in the riding.
Compton is one of the most destitute ridings of Canada. There are various places where something should be done. If we do not act, a number of municipalities would be forced to disappear.
The Lac-Megantic municipality, where I live, is quite important. With a population of 8,000, it has no industries. A few small industries can be found, some of which
July 6, 1972

operate at low speed. There are certainly great needs to be met.
The situation in the city of Coaticook where 8,000 or more people live, is also tragic. Although this municipality is a little more prosperous than Lac-Megantic, it would certainly need other advantages for its development.
Before concluding, Mr. Speaker, I want to express the hope that it will be possible to consider the area in which I live and to meet my request that Sherbrooke become a designated area, or else, that the parishes of Compton be taken out of the Sherbrooke area to become a separate area, so that the population can take advantage of the act.

speakeroldname: Mr. Marcel Prud'homme (Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State of Canada
maintopic: REGIONAL ECONOMIC EXPANSION-REQUEST THAT SHERBROOKE BE DESIGNATED AS SPECIAL AREA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Department of Regional Economic Expansion-whose head is the indefatigable hon. member for Langelier (Mr. Marchand) who, as we know, spares no time or effort to try and eradicate economic disparities between regions-conducts several studies, in co-operation with the Quebec Planning and Development Board, concerning the potential for development of the Eastern Townships area.
A White Paper on development trends in the Eastern Townships area has also been prepared. This document has been prepared jointly by the Department of Regional Economic Expansion, the Quebec Planning and Development Board, and the Regional Development Council.
However, even if studies and discussions are going well, the present "special areas" in Quebec having been designated up to June 30, 1973, the creation of a new "special area" cannot possibly be decided soon.
The hon. member will be happy to learn, however, that review of the policy and programs of the Department of Regional Economic Expansion has been undertaken. In this review, the whole matter of designated areas will be studied very carefully by the department.

maintopic: CONSUMER AFFAIRS-ALLEGED DELAY BY AUTOMOBILE MANUFACTURERS IN RECALLING CARS WITH DEFECTIVE PARTS UNTIL WARRANTIES HAVE EXPIRED

speechtext:
Mr. ]ohn Burton (Regina East): Mr. Speaker, last Tuesday I asked the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Andras) whether his department was investigating cases of large companies, particularly automobile companies, which are possibly delaying recall notices because of defective parts until warranties or a large percentage of them have expired, having the effect of reducing the cost of replacing defective parts to the companies involved.
The reason for my question is a representation by a constituent in possession of a 1967 automobile. This man found he had a defective engine-mount part and subsequently learned by Canadian Press dispatch dated December 7, 1971, that General Motors had announced that the recall involved V-8 engines only. This was in regard to GM cars. It covered 1965 through 1969 regular sized Chevrolets and Novas as well as 1967 through 1969 regular sized Camaros and certain light trucks.
I understand from this release and articles appearing in various automotive publications that the recalled vehicles must still be covered by the General Motors' warranty. I understand there may be some confusion with regard to
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion
the extent to which they would be covered by the warranty. The person who contacted me informed me he received a letter on April 4, 1972, some four months after General Motors had announced it was recalling certain vehicles. That was after this person had made an inquiry of General Motors Corporation. I quote from the letter he received dated April 4, 1972:
We would take this opportunity to explain that in the very near future, a letter will be sent to the owners of all 1967 Chevrolet automobiles involved in the engine mount recall, explaining the procedures to be followed for the installation of an engine restraint device.
If the particular vehicle has exceeded the warranty limits, the inspection or replacement of any broken mounts will be the owner's expense, whereas the restraining device will be installed at no charge to the owner, regardless of time or mileage.
It seems to me this matter warrants investigation. I want to make clear I am not necessarily making charges against the automobile company involved; I am simply suggesting this is a case which warrants investigation, because it seems to me if the automobile company delays sending out recall notices it has the effect of reducing the liability of the automobile company in replacing the defective parts.
In this particular case I was informed by letter dated May 31 that this man had still not received his recall notice. That was almost six months after General Motors had issued its press release saying that these automobiles would be recalled. Thus, I think this is a matter which should be investigated by the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs. I want to say I appreciate the response of the Minister when he said he was prepared to look into the matter. I wanted to take the time this evening to elaborate on the facts of the case.

speakeroldname: Mr. Gaston Clermont (Parliamentary Secretary to President of the Treasury Board):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Treasury Board
maintopic: CONSUMER AFFAIRS-ALLEGED DELAY BY AUTOMOBILE MANUFACTURERS IN RECALLING CARS WITH DEFECTIVE PARTS UNTIL WARRANTIES HAVE EXPIRED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in replying to the hon. member for Regina East (Mr. Burton) on behalf of the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Duquet) I would like to make it very clear that my answer is limited to the responsibility of automobile manufacturers where recalls are initiated.
Under section 8 of the Motor Vehicle Safety Act, manufacturers, importers or distributors of motor vehicles are required to give notification of any defects in the construction, design or functioning of motor vehicles or their components which affect or are likely to affect the safe operation of those vehicles and of which the manufacturers, distributors or importers are aware. This notification of defects must be given to dealers and to subsequent purchasers of the motor vehicle in a prescribed manner.
While the conditions of section 8 of the Motor Vehicle Safety Act are only applicable to vehicles after the act was proclaimed on January 1, 1971, manufacturers do by virtue of other legal obligations follow this practice rigidly with respect to vehicles which were produced prior to that date. Thus, the notification of safety defects or recall campaign procedure is not related to the period of warranty to the production. To the best of our knowledge, manufacturers have been accepting responsibility for the cost of correcting such defects where the problems have been related to the design or production methods and the length of warranty is not in question.
